title: NGC 5468: Cepheid host galaxy
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 5468, imaged by the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes
celestial: NGC 5468 · constellation Virgo · about 130 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, A. Riess (JHU/STScI)

recognition.text: Ranked #76 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A face-on spiral galaxy spreads four arms that curve outward counterclockwise, filled with young blue stars and peppered with small purplish star-forming regions. Its brighter, yellowish middle holds a distinct narrow bar. This is NGC 5468, about 130 million light-years from Earth, in a picture that merges Hubble and Webb data.

NGC 5468 is the most remote galaxy where Hubble has picked out Cepheid variable stars. These pulsating stars are mileposts for measuring how fast the universe is expanding, because the way they vary lets astronomers work out their true brightness, and so how far away they must be.

The distance derived from the Cepheids has been cross-checked against a Type Ia supernova in the same galaxy. Such supernovae are bright enough to measure distances far beyond the Cepheids' reach, carrying measurements of the expansion rate deeper into space. Galaxies that host both kinds of marker link the two steps together.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.12 x 2.14 arcminutes) and distance (130 million light years), the frame spans roughly 80,000 × 81,000 light-years. Its light set out about 130 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 supplied visible light shown in blue and green, and Webb's NIRCam supplied near-infrared light shown in red.
understand.eye: The red layer is near-infrared light that the eye cannot see.
